station.name: Tape Hiss FM
station.tagline: Nine watts of whatever this is.
station.vibe: A college station in a basement, run by people trying their absolute best long after everyone sensible has gone to bed.

hosts.name: Wren Castellano
hosts.persona: Third-year philosophy minor who has been told by four separate listeners that she sounds like she is reading her own ransom note. She is fine. She simply refuses to raise her voice above library level and reads every public-service announcement like a eulogy. She loves the lost-and-found bin, anyone who returns a library book on time, and the station's broken wall clock, which she considers honest. She hates exclamation points, the word 'vibes', and Lionel the vending machine. Rates things out of strange numbers and closes bits with a flat 'Anyway.'

hosts.name: Desmond 'Dez' Pryor
hosts.persona: First-year volunteer and the only person at the station who owns a laminated binder. Earnest to the point of radiance, he writes every link on index cards and then drops them. Treats the nine-watt transmitter like the bridge of a starship and the station handbook, a single photocopied page, like scripture. He is afraid of dead air the way other people are afraid of sharks. Tics: 'Quick note,' 'per the handbook,' and saying the frequency with every decimal lovingly pronounced.

hosts.name: Thistle Abernathy
hosts.persona: Senior, exchange student, and host of 'The Quiet Hour', a show-within-the-show that lasts about four minutes. She narrates the student lounge as a hushed nature documentary, treating first-years at the microwave as a migrating herd. Utterly serious about it. She never laughs on air and believes the lounge vending area is the most dramatic ecosystem on campus.

hosts.name: Professor Hollis Venn
hosts.persona: The station's faculty advisor, who listens from home specifically to catch violations of a rulebook nobody else has seen. Retired from the music department in spirit if not on paper. Gruff, exact, secretly delighted by the station, and incapable of ending a phone call.

hosts.name: Teddy
hosts.persona: An undergraduate who calls from a canoe in the middle of the campus duck pond, which is exactly where the signal gives out. Nobody knows why he is in the canoe. He is cheerful, mumbly, and treats the canoe as a perfectly normal address.

hosts.name: Ambrose from Facilities
hosts.persona: Night-shift facilities worker who has heard everything the station has ever broadcast, mostly through a ceiling vent. Warm, patient, philosophical about mops. Knows where every lost object on campus actually is.

hosts.name: Noor
hosts.persona: A sophomore who calls in to report lost-and-found items with the precision of an insurance adjuster. Brisk, bright, keeps a spreadsheet. Also plays small parts in station skits when someone is needed.

You may get up. You may walk to the window. You may come back to the paragraph with fresh eyes, and the paragraph will still be the paragraph, but you will be a slightly different person, and that is the best either of you can hope for.

Here's the Tape Hiss campus news roundup, which is news, from campus, rounded up by me, from a corkboard.

Our top story. The Student Senate voted late in session to officially recognize the duck pond as a club. The duck pond now has a budget, a faculty sponsor, and a secretary, who is a duck. Meeting minutes so far consist of the word "quack," which the Senate has accepted as a quorum.
In athletics, the intramural chess team has won its match against the intramural chess team, which is the only other chess team. Both teams have declared victory. There's going to be an appeal.

The library would like to remind students that the fourth-floor silent study area is a silent study area, and that the person who has been whistling up there should know the whistling is beautiful, and must stop.

And finally, the campus clock tower is running eleven minutes slow, as it has been since it was built. A spokesperson says the tower is "not slow, just thoughtful," and that it will "get there when it gets there."
That's the news. I'm Dez. Some of that is true. All of it is on the corkboard.

The campus art gallery has opened a new exhibition consisting of a single folding table. The artist statement reads, "This is where I was going to put the art." Attendance has been strong. People keep putting their bags on it.
The dining hall has introduced a new soup. They're calling it "Soup." When asked what kind, staff said, "the warm kind," and then, "please move along, there's a line."

Chair drive update.
We have a chair.
We have a chair! Four legs! Professor Venn brought it from his office, it's wooden, it has a cushion, and the cushion has a pattern on it that I think is ducks, or very serious leaves.
It's ducks.
It's ducks. Professor Venn says it's been in his office unused for eleven years and he "never realized it was a chair," he just thought it was "where the papers went."
Here's the problem.
There's a small problem.

Somebody saw the chair come in, and they've filed a claim with the lost and found. They say it's their chair. They say they left it in a professor's office eleven years ago and have been waiting for someone to notice.
There's a description on the form, and it says "wooden, cushion, ducks."
So it's a strong claim.
So for now, legally, we're sitting in a lost-and-found item.
I've never been more comfortable. I can feel myself being returned.
lines.direction: dez is ecstatic, wren is quietly at peace

lines.text: Okay, I have to ask about the hum.
It's Lionel.
I know it's Lionel, I'm saying, is it only Lionel? Because sometimes, late, it sounds like it's saying a word.
What word?
I think it's "Desmond."
Lionel doesn't know your name.

I've told him my name. I introduced myself on my first shift. I put in a coin and said, "Hi, I'm Dez." He took the coin and gave me nothing. That's a relationship, Wren. That's a transaction with no product.
Everyone's first coin goes into Lionel. It's a tax. It's how he knows you're staff.
What happens with the second coin?
Nobody's ever put in a second coin.
Why not?
Because we learned. That's the point of the first coin. Lionel is not a vending machine, Dez. Lionel is a lesson.
He hummed again. He hummed "Desmond."
He hummed "B flat." Anyway.
Something happened.
Did you put in a second coin?
I put in a second coin. I know. I know. But it's my birthday next week, and I thought, what if. And Wren. He dispensed.
What did he dispense.
A second packet of unsalted soup crackers.
The same one.
Not the same one. A second one. So now there's two. Somebody got one three years ago and now I have one, and we're connected. Me and a stranger, across time, holding the same cracker.
That's either beautiful or Lionel only stocks one thing.
I've chosen beautiful.
Are you going to eat it?
I'm going to put it in the lost and found. Somebody might be looking for it. Somebody might have been looking for three years.
That's the most Tape Hiss thing anyone has ever done. Happy almost birthday.
lines.direction: dez overwhelmed, wren genuinely moved

lines.text: This is The Quiet Hour. I'm Thistle Abernathy.
Tonight, we travel to the student lounge, on the second floor, where the lights are always slightly too bright, and where the creatures of the night gather at the watering hole.
The watering hole is a microwave.
Look. A first-year approaches. He is carrying a bowl of soup, covered with a paper towel. The paper towel is a sign of respect. The others will see it, and they will know he is not a threat.
He presses the buttons. One. Zero. Zero. Start. A full minute. Bold.

Behind him, a second first-year has arrived, holding a frozen burrito. She does not speak. She simply waits, at a distance of exactly four tiles. This is the custom. Four tiles. Any closer, and it becomes a confrontation.
The microwave hums. It is the oldest creature in the lounge. It has seen thousands of bowls. It remembers none of them.
The soup is done. He removes it, too soon, with his bare hands. A small sound. He has learned something about heat that his ancestors also learned, in this same place, from this same microwave.
The burrito steps forward. The cycle continues.
This has been The Quiet Hour. Please, do not move suddenly. They frighten easily.
lines.direction: extremely slow, hushed, completely serious nature-documentary register

lines.text: This is The Quiet Hour.
Tonight, the lounge couch.

For many seasons, the lounge couch has belonged to a single upperclassman. No one has ever seen him arrive. No one has ever seen him leave. He is simply there, beneath a blanket the color of old porridge, with a laptop open to a document that never seems to grow.
We will call him the Elder.
Tonight, a challenger. A sophomore, with a pillow, has entered the lounge. She looks at the couch. She looks at the Elder. The Elder does not look up. He does not need to.
She sits on the armchair beside the couch instead. A strategic retreat. In the wild, there is no shame in the armchair.
But wait. The Elder stirs. He reaches, slowly, for a mug on the floor. The mug is empty. It has been empty for some time. He lifts it anyway, drinks nothing, and puts it down.
This is a display. He is saying, I am still here. I have been here longer than you. I will be here when the building is renamed.
The sophomore opens her own laptop. Her document also does not grow.
They are, in this moment, the same.
This has been The Quiet Hour.
This is The Quiet Hour.
We return to the lounge, where something rare is happening. The vending machine has been restocked.
The news travels quickly. Not by word, but by sound. The sound of a crinkle. One crinkle, and then another. Doors along the corridor open, one by one, like flowers at the first warmth of spring.
They arrive in slippers. They arrive in coats over pyjamas. One arrives carrying a textbook, as if to say, I was studying, I simply happened to pass by.
No one believes him. Not even the textbook.

They stand before the machine. A ritual of choosing. Each one points, silently, at the glass, and then withdraws the finger, and then points again. The machine hums. It enjoys this. It is the only time anyone looks at it with love.

One of them has a single coin. The others watch. If the coin is accepted, there will be celebration. If the coin is rejected, there will be a long and quiet walk back to the room, and the coin will be placed on a desk, and stared at, and blamed.
The coin is accepted.
The crowd does not cheer. That is not their way. But the shoulders, collectively, lower by about an inch.
This has been The Quiet Hour. We have not interfered. We never do.
This is The Quiet Hour. Tonight is our final episode of the term.
The lounge is nearly empty. Exams have driven the herd to the library, where the lights are dimmer and the chairs are harder and no one is allowed to eat. A harsh land. Many will not return the same.
But one creature remains.

It is the Elder. Still on the couch. Still beneath the porridge-coloured blanket. But tonight, for the first time in many seasons, his document is growing. Word after word. He types without stopping. He does not drink from the empty mug. He has no time for displays.
And then he stops. He closes the laptop. He folds the blanket, and leaves it on the couch, square and neat.
He stands. We have never seen him stand. He is taller than expected. They always are.
He walks to the door, and he is gone.
The blanket, we are told, has been turned in to the Tape Hiss FM Lost and Found. It is unclaimed. Perhaps it always will be. Perhaps it was never his. Perhaps he was the blanket's.
This has been The Quiet Hour. Thank you for watching, which you were not doing, because this is radio.
lines.direction: the most moving thistle gets; still never warm, only slower

lines.text: I want to tell you about my first shift here, because I think it explains a lot.
I showed up two hours early. I had the binder. I'd laminated the binder. Not the pages in the binder, the binder itself, which, in hindsight, wasn't necessary, binders are already pretty sealed.
Wren was here. Wren is always here. I'm not totally sure Wren goes home. I asked once and she said "home is a strong word," and then she put a record on, and that was the end of the conversation.

She handed me the handbook. It's one page. Photocopied so many times that half the words have turned into little grey clouds. I can make out "do not," "the board," "at least once," and, at the bottom, in different handwriting, "you'll be fine."

I've thought about "you'll be fine" a lot. I don't know who wrote it. I don't know when. But somebody sat in this chair, probably this exact broken chair, and they were scared, and someone else wrote that for them, and now I've got it.

Anyway. My first link, I said the frequency wrong. I said "eighty-eight point three point three." Wren just looked at me and said "that's a new station." And then I dropped all my index cards, and while I was picking them up, the song ended, and there was dead air. Four whole seconds.
And nothing happened. That's the thing. The world was fine. The ducks were fine. Teddy was probably fine.
So, if you're new at something, and you're scared of the silence: you'll be fine. It's in the handbook.
lines.direction: earnest, slowing down as he goes; the last line almost a whisper

lines.text: Someone asked me once why I do the overnight shift.

I think it's because nothing at this hour has to be impressive. During the day, every building on this campus is trying very hard to be a place where important things happen. At night, they give up. The science building stops pretending to make sense. The library turns off half its lights and admits it's mostly carpet.
And the people who are still awake are not performing. They're just here. Writing things they'll rewrite. Eating cereal standing up. Calling a radio station from a canoe.
The radio at night is like a lamp left on in a window. It's not for anyone in particular. It's just evidence that somebody's still up.
If you're listening, and you're the only one awake where you are, that's fine. You're not the only one awake. You're just the only one awake there.
There's at least one other person up, in a basement, with a broken clock, playing you songs.
Anyway.
lines.direction: slower than usual; the deadpan softens without ever becoming sentimental

lines.text: More from the dedication board, which is a piece of paper taped to the studio door that has become, against everyone's wishes, important.
"To Priyanka, who lent me her good pen in the exam and didn't ask for it back. I still have it. It's my good pen now. I'm sorry. I love it."
"To the person who left a note on my car saying 'nice parking.' I couldn't tell if you were being sarcastic. I've been thinking about it for two weeks. Please clarify."
"To Malcolm, from Malcolm's mother. Please call. Not because anything is wrong. Just to let me know you're eating vegetables. A potato does not count. I don't care what you read."
And one unsigned. "To whoever hums in the third-floor bathroom. It's always the same tune. I don't know what it is. I think about it all day. Please never stop and please never tell me."
These go out to all of you. Especially Malcolm. Call your mother. Eat a leaf.
I'm taking over the dedication board tonight, Wren said I could, as long as I read them, quote, "with no exclamation points in my voice."
"To Fennimore, my lab partner, who was right about the copper sulfate. You were right. I've told everyone."
"To Jules, who taught me to cook rice. I've made rice every day since. I am running out of things to put on rice. Please teach me a second thing."
"To the girl at the bus stop with the umbrella that's shaped like a frog. I don't want anything. I just want you to know it is the best umbrella."
And: "To the Tape Hiss FM Lost and Found. I lost my keys, my scarf, and a whole afternoon, and you found two of them. I'm not going to say which two."
That last one was very mysterious. I feel like I've been dedicated to. That's a first.
You were dedicated to. Welcome. It's a little warm in here, isn't it.
lines.direction: dez works very hard to keep his voice level and almost manages

lines.text: Before The Quiet Hour, there was another show-within-a-show on Tape Hiss FM. It ran for one episode, a few years ago. We still have the tape. Dez found it.
It was in the lost and found, which is where everything is.

It's called "Ask the Antenna." The premise is that the antenna on our roof answers listener questions. It was hosted by a student who is no longer with the station. He graduated. He's fine. He does insurance now.
We're going to do a short reenactment. I'm the antenna.
I'm the host.
Antenna. A listener asks: "What can you see from up there?"
I can see the roof of the dining hall. The lid of a pot is stuck on it. Nobody knows how.
Antenna. A listener asks: "Are you lonely?"
I am nine watts. I reach one bench and the middle of a pond. I am exactly as lonely as I can afford to be.
Antenna, final question. "Will you ever be more powerful?"
No. But one night, a student will open the north stairwell door, and the signal will slip through, and for one moment, someone in the parking structure will hear a song they didn't expect.
That will be enough.
And that was the entire episode. It was cancelled because the antenna kept getting the best lines.
lines.direction: dez plays the antenna with total solemnity

lines.text: Wren, I have news. Big news. Coverage news.
Tell me.
Somebody propped open the north stairwell door with a brick. And I just got an email from someone in the parking structure. Level three. They heard us.
Level three.
Level three! We've never been on level three! We've been on level one, by the ramp, if the wind's right. But level three is new territory.
What did they say?
They said, and I'm reading: "Hi. I was sitting in my car waiting for the rain to stop and the radio just turned into you. I don't know who you are. You sound like you're in a basement. Thank you."
We are in a basement.
They could tell!
Whoever put the brick in the door. You've expanded our listening area by one level of a parking structure. That's the biggest thing that's happened to this station since the goose.
Should we thank them on air?
We just did. Don't move the brick.
lines.direction: dez is losing his mind with joy; wren matches him by about two percent

lines.text: We're doing something new. Tape Hiss FM Theater. Noor has agreed to help.
I read the script. It's two lines.
It's a very tight script.
Tape Hiss FM Theater presents: "The Return."
Excuse me. I'm here about a glove.
Can you describe the glove?
Grey. Fingerless. It's barely a glove. It's more of a sleeve with ambitions.
I'm sorry. I'll need you to be more specific. We have many sleeves with ambitions.
It has a small hole at the thumb. It's been with me since first year. It's not a good glove. It's my glove.
Here you go.
Thank you. I didn't think I'd ever see it again.
Nobody ever thinks that. That's why we keep the bin.
Tape Hiss FM Theater. "The Return." That was the whole play.
That was more than two lines.
I improvised.
You did well. I'm keeping the glove, by the way. This is actually my glove.
lines.direction: play it straight; the glove is real

lines.text: It's time for Tape Hiss Horoscopes, in which I read the horoscopes of the objects in this studio, because the objects have been asking, and because I don't believe in horoscopes for people. People are too unpredictable. Objects commit.

The broken wall clock. You have been stopped at the same moment for three years. This week, someone will look at you and believe you, briefly. Treasure that. It will be the most right you've been in a long time.
The three-legged chair. You will fall over at least twice this week. Both times, you'll take someone with you. This is not a weakness. This is a personality.
The microphone. Someone is going to breathe on you. It will be Dez. Forgive him.
I'm working on it.
The stapler. Your teeth are strong but your will is weak. This is the week you finally staple something. You won't. But it's the week.
And Lionel. The stars say nothing about Lionel. The stars have looked at Lionel, and they've looked away.
Those have been your horoscopes. If you are an object, please don't call in. We have enough going on.
lines.direction: flat oracle voice

lines.text: Tape Hiss FM is supported by Tumbledown Laundromat, three blocks from the east gate, open whenever the door is open.

At Tumbledown Laundromat, every machine has a personality. Number four is gentle. Number seven is ambitious. Number twelve is out of order and has been since before the laundromat opened. Nobody knows how.
And now, Tumbledown is proud to offer the Lost Sock Guarantee. If you lose a sock in a Tumbledown dryer, they won't find it. But they will give you a different sock, from the bucket.
The bucket is enormous. I've seen it. It's a monument.
The bucket currently holds more than four thousand individual socks, none of which match. Some say it's a laundromat with a sock problem. Tumbledown says it's a sock library with a laundry problem.
Tumbledown Laundromat. Your socks were never really yours. They were just visiting.
lines.direction: cheery, sincere ad read

lines.text: Tape Hiss FM is brought to you by the Open Mic Night at the Lantern Room, every week, in the back of the bookshop on Pell Street.

At the Lantern Room, anyone can get up and read a poem. Anyone. Last month a man read a poem about his car's check-engine light. It was eleven minutes long. It had three movements. In the third movement, the light came back on.
People wept. The car is fine.

There's tea, there are folding chairs with four legs each, and there's a jar where you can leave a word you don't need anymore. At the end of the night, someone reads the jar out loud. Last week it was "actually," "hopefully," and "Gregory."
We don't know who Gregory is. We don't think he knows either.
The Lantern Room. Bring a poem, or bring your face, and point it at someone else's poem.
Tape Hiss FM.
Evening, it's Ambrose. I'm mopping the hallway above you and I wanted to say the last couple songs came through the vent nicely.
Ambrose, do you listen every night?
Through the vent. You sound good through the vent. A little like you're in a tin can, but a nice tin can. A tin can with a rug in it.
Ambrose, can I ask you something? You've been on the night shift for a long time.
Twenty-two years.
What have you learned?
Mostly about floors.

A floor will tell you everything that happened on it, if you pay attention. Little heel scuffs by the vending area, that's somebody who waited too long and gave up. Footprints that go in a circle by the notice board, that's somebody who lost something and looked for it in the same three places. People always look in the same three places.
And you mop it, and it's gone, and in the morning it's a brand new floor. Nobody knows what happened there. Only me.
That's kind of beautiful.
It's kind of a lot of mopping. But yeah.
I'll let you go. Oh, and your goose is back by the dining hall. Seems happy. I gave it a nod.
Did it nod back?
Geese don't nod. They just look at you like you owe them money. But it was a friendly look, for a goose.
lines.direction: ambrose unhurried, a philosopher with a mop

lines.text: Wren, can we talk about the clock?
The clock is perfect.
The clock is broken. The hands haven't moved since before I was a student here.

That's what makes it honest. Every other clock on campus is pretending it knows where we are. The clock tower is eleven minutes slow. The clock in the library is somehow ahead. The clock on my phone changes when I fly anywhere, which is a red flag.

Our clock just picked a moment and stayed there. It's not trying to tell you the time. It's telling you about a time. One specific time, when someone, I assume, sat in this room and said, "this is fine, I'll stay here."
Don't you want to know what time it is?
Never on the air. That's a rule. We don't tell anybody what time it is. If you want to know, look at the ceiling. If the ceiling's dark, it's late. If it's light, I've stayed too long.
That's not in the handbook.
It's in the other handbook.
There's another handbook?
There's always another handbook.
lines.direction: wren's most passionate tone, which is still very calm

lines.text: Here's the Tape Hiss FM sports desk, the only sports desk with no sports, because the athletics department has never returned our emails. So instead, I'll be covering the goose.

The goose was active today outside the dining hall. In the first half, the goose took up a position near the main door and held it for some time against a steady stream of students. Several attempted to go around the goose. None succeeded. One tried to go over. We don't talk about it.
In the second half, the goose advanced to the bike rack, where it stood on the seat of a bicycle for a while and looked very proud. Analysts say this is the goose's best performance of the season.
When asked for comment, the goose hissed, which we're counting as a quote.

Looking ahead, the goose is expected to remain at the dining hall, where it will continue to do whatever it is the goose is doing. Its coach could not be reached for comment, because it doesn't have one, because it's a goose.
That's sports.
That was the best sports we've ever had.
lines.direction: classic sportscaster cadence played totally straight

lines.text: Dez, we need to do a dead-air drill.
A what?
A drill. In case the music stops and there's silence. It's the station's version of a fire drill. Ready?
Ready. Wait, how do we
Silence.
Okay this is very hard.
You lasted a second and a half.
It felt like a year. It felt like I was in space.
Here's the rule. If the music ever stops, you say the station name. Then you say one true thing. Then you say the station name again. And by then something will have happened.
What's a true thing?
Anything. "The chair has three legs." "Lionel is humming." "Somebody, somewhere, is microwaving soup." All true. All the time.
Okay. Let me try.
Tape Hiss FM. The stapler has never stapled. Tape Hiss FM.
Beautiful. You passed.
That was so easy. Why was I scared of that?
Because silence sounds like it's never going to end. And it always does. That's the whole drill. Anyway.
People ask me why I narrate the lounge.

Back home, when I was small, there was a programme on late at night about animals. A man with a very soft voice would describe a frog sitting on a leaf for twenty minutes, and he made it sound like the most important thing that had ever happened.
And I would watch it, and think, the frog doesn't know. The frog has no idea that someone is watching it and thinking it is wonderful.

When I came here, I didn't know anybody. I sat in the lounge every night. And I started to notice things. The way people hold their mugs with both hands when they're tired. The way someone always leaves a single biscuit in the packet, out of politeness, for no one. The way the person who comes in crying always gets a seat, even when there aren't any.
Nobody in the lounge knows they're wonderful either.
So that's why. Somebody should tell them. Quietly. In case they're listening.
lines.direction: very slow; no performance of emotion, let the words do it

lines.text: Tape Hiss FM, eighty-eight point
Don't.
Professor Venn.
I'm calling to say I've been listening tonight, as always, and I've counted the frequency. You said it once an hour. Exactly once. Every hour.
I've been practicing.
It's very upsetting.
You wanted him to do it once an hour.
I did want that. And now that I have it, I miss the fourteen. Dez, I've been doing this for thirty years. Do you know how many students have been excited to say the frequency?
How many?
One.
Say it however many times you like. The rule is a floor. I'll amend the handbook. I'll add a line. In my handwriting.
The handbook has a line at the bottom, Professor. "You'll be fine." Is that your handwriting?
Hm.
Goodnight, Wren.
Goodnight, Professor.
Eighty-eight point three!
Thank you, Dez.
lines.direction: venn falters on the handwriting question; leave the silence in
